title: Partition, Prompt, Aggregate: Statistical Self-Consistency in Language Models
claim: Aggregating estimates from recursively partitioned subgroups via total probability yields reconstructed marginals that can be checked against direct estimates and ground truth.
layout: 4 stages left-to-right, binary tree center, arrows to aggregates then evaluation
description: A four-stage left-to-right pipeline with a caption under each stage. At left, a green question box asks for the probability that yearly income is above $50k. A dashed arrow runs from it to the second tree level. Pink and purple context bubbles ("at least 20 years old" and "younger than 20 years") label the two branches below the root. In the center, a binary tree with four levels of circles sits on grey bands. The circles shade from white to black green. Horizontal arrows lead from each level to a column of circles on the right. These circles turn into pie charts that are split more finely at each level, which shows the reconstructed aggregates. A bracket merges them and points to two grey boxes. One shows the root estimate and the other shows ground truth (a check mark). Each box has a "?=" sign in front of it. The eye goes first to the colorful tree and the context bubbles.
caption: Reconstructing aggregate estimates from subpopulation estimates. A binary tree recursively partitions a base population into increasingly specific subpopulations. For each subpopulation, we elicit an LLM estimate by verbalizing the split criteria in context, then reconstruct population-level aggregate estimates at each level via the law of total probability. We compare the reconstructed aggregates against the model's direct marginal estimate to assess self-consistency, and against ground-truth population data to assess alignment.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often used to perform a form of conditional inference. In-context learning is one implicit way to do this. The prompt specifies a context and the model's output is treated as an estimate of the corresponding conditional distribution. If this interpretation holds, then LLM estimates should satisfy basic probabilistic identities. In particular, the law of total probability asserts that prior-weighted conditional distributions aggregate into population-level marginals over any valid partition of the population. In this work, we investigate to what extent LLM estimates adhere to this self-consistency principle. We use binary trees as an evaluation scaffold to recursively partition a population into increasingly fine-grained subpopulations. We then prompt LLMs with verbalized subpopulation descriptions in context, aggregate the resulting estimates back into population-level estimates, and compare them across partitions of varying granularity. Translating these comparisons into a benchmark score and evaluating frontier models across problem domains, we demonstrate widespread violations of basic consistency properties. An in-depth study of persona prompting further reveals a pattern we call the macro fallacy: estimates reconstructed from more fine-grained subpopulation responses are often better aligned with human reference data than direct population-level estimates. The effect persists across variations in partitioning, verbalization, and estimation task, suggesting that models possess relevant subpopulation knowledge but do not reliably propagate it into aggregate estimates. This gap establishes statistical self-consistency as an unsaturated, reference-free criterion for evaluating LLMs.
